newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian August trade figures worrisome - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Indian August trade figures worrisome - analysts.

text.p: India's exports in August showed a growth rate down to 2.38 percent year-on-year compared with 20.66 percent in the same month last year, fueling fears of a slowdown in trade and industry, economic analysts said on Thursday.

According to the commerce ministry, exports in August crawled were $2.60 billion up only slightly from $2.54 billion last year. Imports in August declined by 0.66 percent at $2.9 billion against $2.92 billion last year.
"It is definitely a slowdown. There is a slowdown in trade as well as industry," V. Raghuraman, secretary general of Associated chambers of commerce (Assocham), told Reuters.
"This is worrisome and strengthens fears of a overall economic slowdown," he said.
India's non-oil imports in April-August dipped by 3.2 percent at $1.12 billion compared to $1.16 billion in the same period last year.
Oil imports in the first five months in the current fiscal year beginning April, jumped 39.3 percent at $3.7 billion against $2.7 billion in the same month last year.
"The import compression is a reflection of slow industrial growth, mainly infrastructure," Raghuraman said.
The key six-sector infrastructure rate in April-August was up only 3.5 percent compared to 11.7 percent last year.
India aims to achieve industrial growth of 12 percent in 1996/97 (April-March) compared to 10 percent in 1995/96.
"The target of 12 percent is difficult to achieve," Raghuraman said.
"The slowdown in trade and industry is a cause for concern," Shashanka Bhide, an economist at National Council for Applied Economic Research, said.
"The government needs to do some thinking on the overall economic slowdown," a government official, who asked not to be identified, said.
India's gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 7.0 percent in 1995/96 (April-March), against a forecast 6.2 percent and is expected to grow by 6.6 percent in 1996/97.
Analysts said high interest rates and infrastructural bottlenecks would make it hard to reach the 6.6 percent target for growth in 1996/97.
The trends in industrial growth, trade figures, stock market and corporate earnings forecasts paint a pessimistic outlook of the economy, they said.
Most analysts have forecast a dip in earnings for corporates in the the first six months of the current financial year.
"The capital markets are also down and corporates are not announcing any major investment plans," Raghuraman said.
But Finance Minister P. Chidamabaram said last month that it was too early to predict a slowdown in the economy.
